row.title: The Woman Who Tried to Be Good
row.author: Edna Ferber

plot_extraction.response_text:
A woman with a notorious past leaves the town brothel she owns and buys a cottage in a respectable neighborhood, hoping to live openly and decently among ordinary families. Although she improves her home, keeps house, gardens, dresses more modestly, and even joins a church, the townspeople refuse to accept her. Neighbors avoid her, a woman publicly abandons the pew beside her, and a young mother prevents her child, Snooky, from accepting cookies from her.

During a violent winter storm, Snooky becomes dangerously ill with croup while her father is away and no doctor can be reached. The terrified mother seeks the woman’s help. Drawing on the painful experience of having lost her own baby, the outcast woman takes charge, treats the child, and stays through the night until Snooky is safe.

Despite this act, Snooky’s father orders his wife never to speak to their neighbor again. When the couple later passes her without acknowledgment, the woman realizes that even saving their child has not earned her basic human acceptance. Bitterly defeated, she abandons the cottage and returns to her former establishment, while the self-righteous townspeople cite her failure as proof that women like her can never change.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a communal first-person narrator, speaking chiefly as “we” on behalf of a small town and only occasionally narrowing into the more reflective “I.” This collective voice is central to the style: it creates the atmosphere of an observant, gossip-driven community while also implicating the narrator in its prejudice. The repeated “we noticed,” “we knew,” and “we said” gives the prose the cadence of local consensus, but the narrator’s later regrets—most pointedly, “I wish one of us had just stopped to call good morning”—quietly expose that consensus as cowardly and cruel. The narration is therefore both intimate and satirical, participating in the town’s judgment while gradually revealing its moral failure.

The tone combines warm social comedy, irony, pathos, and restrained indignation. Much of the humor comes from the town’s self-satisfied respectability, from gently exaggerated descriptions, and from the discrepancy between what characters claim and how they behave. Blanche is labeled a “bad woman,” yet behaves with generosity, discipline, competence, and courage; her respectable neighbors, by contrast, are censorious, hypocritical, and uncharitable. This reversal is developed without overt sermonizing. The prose repeatedly allows concrete behavior to contradict conventional labels, making the story’s moral argument through irony. Even the final refrain—“I knew she wouldn’t last!” and “They never do!”—is bitterly double-edged: the townspeople interpret Blanche’s failure as proof of her nature, while the reader understands that they caused it.

The diction mixes polished literary narration with colloquial, period-specific American speech. Narrative passages contain vivid, sometimes ornate phrases such as “the dewy, golden morning,” “the flames of her cosy fire dancing gnomelike on the wall,” and “the intimate, human, neighborly sounds” of summer evenings. Dialogue, however, is brisk and vernacular, using contractions, dropped sounds, slang, and regional constructions: “ain’t,” “darned,” “She don’t draw,” “I don’t know’s you’ll need him,” and “What’s a woman like that want to come into a respectable street for?” This contrast lends the setting social authenticity and differentiates public speech from the narrator’s more shaped, retrospective account. Capitalized designations such as “Very Young Husband” and “Very Young Wife” turn individuals into comic social types, emphasizing their immaturity and their roles within the town’s moral drama.

The syntax is varied and highly rhythmic. Long, cumulative sentences are used for observation, description, and social catalogues, often gathering domestic objects, smells, gestures, and neighborhood customs into a densely textured scene. Short sentences and fragments provide judgment or emotional emphasis: “But we did not.” “My baby died.” “Croup,” said Blanche Devine, “and began her fight.” Parenthetical remarks and dashes reproduce the narrator’s conversational manner, allowing qualifications, jokes, and revealing asides to interrupt the flow. Repetition is also important, especially in phrases such as “The baby! The baby!” and “They never do,” which acquire different emotional meanings as the story progresses.

The descriptive style is strongly sensory and domestic. Clothing, food, household work, gardens, weather, and interiors are rendered with precise visual, tactile, and olfactory detail. Blanche’s mink coat, diamond earrings, extravagant shoes, window-washing clothes, sweet peas, preserves, tea biscuits, and walnut-topped cookies all function as social and psychological evidence. Smell is especially prominent: perfume initially marks her as suspect, while later the scents of baking, pickling, and jam associate her with home, nourishment, and ordinary feminine labor. These details are not merely decorative. They dramatize Blanche’s longing to enter respectable domestic life and show how thoroughly she learns its rituals, even though the community refuses to recognize her transformation.

Characterization is indirect and behavior-based. Blanche’s past is only partially disclosed, largely through Alderman Mooney’s report, while her character emerges through repeated actions: she pays inflated prices without protest, renovates the cottage, cleans meticulously, attempts to attend church, offers cookies to a child, and saves that same child’s life. Small gestures carry substantial emotional weight. The dropped cookies, the closed door, the absent earrings, and Blanche’s silent watching from her porch communicate humiliation and loneliness more powerfully than extended introspection would. Her emotional life is usually inferred from posture, facial expression, or practical activity, giving the sentiment a controlled rather than melodramatic quality.

Dialogue is used both to advance events and to expose hypocrisy. The furnace conversation between Alderman Mooney and the Very Young Husband establishes the town’s hostility while revealing the husband’s double standard: formerly a “sower of wild oats,” he now polices women’s respectability. Blanche’s speech is plain, direct, and competent, particularly during Snooky’s illness. Her imperative sentences—“Stop screaming,” “Get the hot water on,” “Don’t you dare faint!”—contrast with the neighbors’ gossip and moral posturing. She speaks least when most wounded, and this economy makes her dignity and pain more forceful.

Structurally, the narrative unfolds as a sequence of social tests. Blanche enters the neighborhood, attempts domestic respectability, seeks admission to church, reaches toward a child, withdraws under rejection, and finally proves her compassion during the storm. Each episode raises the possibility of acceptance, only for the community to deny it. The plot culminates not in Blanche’s moral redemption—her conduct has already established that—but in the neighbors’ decisive failure to reciprocate her goodness. The storm and croup episode temporarily suspends social boundaries through physical danger, but daylight restores prejudice. This produces a circular ending: Blanche returns to the House with the Closed Shutters, while the town returns to its original judgment, now exposed as self-fulfilling.

The imagery repeatedly contrasts openness and closure, visibility and concealment. Closed shutters represent Blanche’s former exclusion; the renovated cottage, sparkling windows, front porch, and open door represent her attempt to become visible and socially available. Yet the neighbors observe her constantly without truly seeing her. Curtains flutter, eyes peer through windows and fences, and Blanche herself watches communal life from a distance. Boundaries such as doors, shutters, pickets, property lines, and pew aisles embody the social barriers surrounding her. The story’s style thus turns the ordinary architecture of small-town life into a moral geography of belonging and exclusion.

Overall, the prose is humane, ironic, socially observant, and emotionally controlled. It combines the accessibility of oral storytelling with carefully patterned motifs and a sophisticated unreliable collective voice. Its defining effect comes from making the reader see beyond the town’s vocabulary of “good” and “bad”: the community narrates Blanche’s exclusion as common sense, while the accumulation of domestic detail, compassionate action, and understated suffering reveals that its respectable judgment is the story’s true vice.

generation.response_text:
We began talking about Blanche Devine before the paint on her cottage was dry.

The cottage stood on Sycamore Street, between the Dillons’ yellow house and the little gray place rented by the Very Young Husband and the Very Young Wife. Sycamore Street was considered respectable, though not fashionable. We had maples, cement walks, porch swings, lace curtains, children with scabbed knees, and fathers who came home at six carrying folded newspapers and looking as if the nation had been waiting all day for their opinions.

Blanche’s old house stood at the far end of town, beyond the freight tracks, where the street lamps thinned out and respectable women never went. Men called it the House with the Red Curtains when they were speaking among themselves, and “that place” when their wives were near.

We knew all about it, naturally.

That is to say, no two of us knew the same thing, but we had repeated our several versions so often that the result possessed the solidity of Scripture.

Then Blanche sold it—or leased it, Alderman Mooney said; Mooney always knew the legal side of wickedness—and bought the Sycamore Street cottage for forty-two hundred dollars cash.

“She paid four hundred more than it’s worth,” said Mrs. Dillion.

“Five hundred,” corrected Mrs. Mooney.

“Money don’t mean anything to that kind,” said Mrs. Pritchard.

That was one of our first judgments against Blanche: she had paid too much.

The second was her coat.

She came to inspect the cottage in a long brown fur coat, though the day was only October-sharp and not genuinely cold. The fur was soft and dark and had a glistening ripple when she moved. Below it showed two extremely small shoes with heels so high that Mrs. Pritchard declared a Christian woman would break her ankles in them. Blanche wore diamond drops in her ears, and when she passed us there came with her a fragrance of violets, warm skin, and some foreign powder.

“What’s she want over here?” asked Mrs. Dillion, after Blanche had gone through the cottage gate.

That was what troubled us. We could understand Blanche in the shuttered house beyond the tracks. Wickedness ought to have an address. It ought to stay in its district and permit virtue to take another route. But Blanche, walking openly beneath our maples at eleven o’clock in the morning, was like a scarlet flower thrust into a row of white kitchen gardens.

Alderman Mooney met the Very Young Husband at the hardware store that afternoon.

“Heard who’s bought next door to you?” Mooney asked.

The Very Young Husband had heard. He had also heard that Blanche intended to live there alone and respectable.

“Can she do that?” he demanded.

“Bought the property, didn’t she?”

“I don’t mean legally. I mean—well, darn it, Mooney, I’ve got a wife.”

We smiled afterward when Mooney repeated this, because the Very Young Husband had not always guarded female innocence with such a flaming sword. Before his marriage he had been celebrated for sowing enough wild oats to seed the county. Marriage, however, had transformed him into a stern agricultural reformer.

“You know her?” Mooney asked him slyly.

“Know her! Certainly not.”

“Thought maybe you might’ve seen her around.”

“I may have passed her somewhere. A man passes all kinds.”

That settled the moral position of Sycamore Street.

Blanche took possession on the first of November.

For three weeks carpenters, paperhangers, plumbers, and painters went in and out. She had the porch repaired, the sagging fence straightened, and the shutters removed from every window. She had the front room done in cream, the dining room in a warm yellow, and the kitchen painted white—white walls, white cupboards, white table, white enamel stove. Mrs. Dillion’s hired girl was engaged to help scrub, and afterward she told us that Blanche had gone over the pantry shelves herself with hot soda water until her hands were red.

“Acts like she never seen dirt before,” the girl said.

“Or like she’s seen too much,” said Mrs. Dillion, and we appreciated that remark.

Blanche’s furniture arrived in vans. Some of it was flamboyant: a carved mahogany bed, velvet chairs, a gilt mirror too large for the parlor. But other pieces were plain and curiously girlish—a white sewing table, a maple rocker, a little desk with pigeonholes. There were pictures, too. Not the sort we expected, but a field of poppies, a blue river under willows, and a print of a mother bending above a child.

She put muslin curtains at the kitchen windows and cream net in the front room. By evening the cottage shone clear and golden among the bare trees. One could see Blanche moving inside, setting a lamp straight, arranging books, carrying a bowl of apples from room to room until she found the proper table for it.

We watched from behind our curtains.

She had opened all her windows.

We had closed ours.

The first morning after she moved in, Blanche appeared in the yard at half past seven wearing a blue gingham dress, a man’s old sweater, and flat shoes. The diamonds were gone. So was the perfume. Her hair, which we had thought naturally arranged in shining waves, was tied up in a cloth.

She swept the porch, shook rugs, polished the front windows, and then attacked the back garden. The place had been neglected. Dead stalks leaned over one another; burdock flourished against the shed; last summer’s beans hung in gray rattling pods. Blanche pulled, dug, burned, and hauled until noon. She worked with a fierce absorption, as though the roots under Sycamore Street were enemies that could be defeated by strength.

“She’ll tire of it,” we said.

But she did not.

All winter she kept that cottage as if expecting the governor’s wife at any moment. Her steps were swept before ours. Her windows flashed on the coldest mornings. Monday brought white sheets snapping on the line; Tuesday, the fragrant steam of ironing; Wednesday, the beating of rugs. By February Blanche had learned to bake bread. Her first loaves were low and stubborn, but she kept on until handsome brown domes cooled beneath clean towels in her kitchen.

The smells that came from her house changed our opinion of her only in detail.

At first there had been violets and expensive scent. Now there were onions browning in butter, coffee, beeswax, cinnamon, yeast, hot starch, and, once, the rich solemn odor of a beef stew that caused Mr. Dillion to ask what they were having next door.

“You’d better go over and find out,” said Mrs. Dillion.

He did not ask again.

Blanche tried friendliness. That was embarrassing.

She nodded when she met us. The first few times she even said, “Good morning.” Her voice was lower than we expected and without any of the bold laughter we had imagined. Mrs. Mooney returned the greeting once, by mistake, then spent the afternoon explaining that politeness meant nothing.

When Blanche encountered Mrs. Pritchard at the grocer’s, she stepped aside to let her pass.

“After you,” Blanche said.

Mrs. Pritchard brushed by as though Blanche had proposed something indecent involving the canned peaches.

The Very Young Wife was the nearest neighbor. She was nineteen, soft-faced, easily frightened, and the mother of Snooky, who was three and believed every fence built expressly for climbing. Blanche could see Snooky playing from her kitchen window. We knew because we often saw her standing there, hands in dishwater, watching him with a look that made us uneasy.

Snooky had yellow hair, a stubborn lower lip, and a red wool cap with a tassel. He called all dogs “Buster” and all women “Lady.” Before his mother learned to prevent it, he waved at Blanche.

“Hello, Lady!”

Blanche would wave back with a wet hand.

The Very Young Wife began keeping him in the rear yard.

In March Blanche appeared at the Methodist church.

We had not expected that. Our churches were open to sinners in the theological sense, but we preferred them washed, anonymous, and from some other street.

She came before the bell stopped ringing and sat near the rear, wearing a dark gray suit and a small black hat. No fur, no diamonds, no trace of violets. Her gloves were plain. She carried a prayer book. If she had entered loudly, or dressed too richly, or shown embarrassment, we could have forgiven ourselves more easily. But she slipped into the pew with such hopeful quiet that the whole congregation seemed suddenly noisy with programs, coughs, and skirts.

Mrs. Pritchard was already seated at the other end of that pew.

For perhaps ten seconds she remained. Then she saw Blanche.

Mrs. Pritchard gathered her handbag, hymn book, gloves, and offended purity. She rose, squeezed past three people, and marched to the opposite side of the aisle. We all observed it. Blanche observed it too.

She looked down at her hands.

During the first hymn she sang. During the second her lips scarcely moved. When the minister preached on the woman taken in sin, several of us thought the selection awkward, though afterward he maintained the sermon had been planned weeks before. Blanche sat motionless beneath his phrases concerning repentance and mercy.

She left before the benediction.

The following Sunday the back pew was empty.

Blanche did not come again.

Spring softened Sycamore Street. The maples put forth small green fans. Rugs bloomed on clotheslines; screens were repaired; men came out after supper to examine lawns as though conducting military inspections. The intimate life of the street moved onto porches. Spoons clicked in lemonade glasses. Babies fretted. Women called children home. Radios sang through open windows. From yard to yard drifted gossip, tobacco smoke, lilac scent, frying ham, and the comfortable laughter of people who know exactly where they belong.

Blanche made a garden.

She planted sweet peas along the fence, nasturtiums beneath the kitchen windows, and rows of lettuce, radishes, parsley, beans, and tomatoes behind the house. She worked in a broad straw hat and faded dress. Her arms browned. She grew stouter, perhaps because of the bread and puddings she was always experimenting with, and the sharp, glittering beauty she had possessed in the fur coat became softer. Once Mrs. Dillion admitted that Blanche looked almost motherly.

“Don’t be fooled,” said Mrs. Pritchard.

We were not.

Yet the garden flourished. Blanche tied her sweet peas with strips of old stocking. She dusted the beans, pinched the tomatoes, and went out at dusk with a tin can to hunt cutworms. We knew every detail because our fences, though excellent for exclusion, were poor protection against eyesight.

Sometimes she sat alone on the porch after dark. Her hands rested idle in her lap while Sycamore Street hummed around her. No one called across. No one asked whether her peas needed rain. No child ran up her steps. She was in the middle of us and farther away than she had been beyond the tracks.

In June she made cookies.

We learned afterward that they were molasses cookies, cut in scalloped circles, with half a walnut pressed into each one. Blanche had put them on a wire rack by the open kitchen window. Snooky smelled them, or perhaps merely saw them. At three years old he had not yet acquired our gift for ignoring what he wanted.

He came through a loose picket.

Blanche was kneeling beside the sweet peas when he appeared.

“Hello, Lady,” said Snooky.

“Hello yourself.”

“What you got?”

“Mud on my knees.”

“No. In there.”

“Cookies.”

“I like cookies.”

Blanche sat back on her heels. She looked toward the Very Young Wife’s house. No one was visible.

“Well,” she said, “that’s fortunate.”

She went inside and returned with two cookies on a blue saucer. Snooky took one in each hand. He had bitten a perfect crescent from the first when his mother came around the house.

“Snooky!”

The boy turned, his mouth full.

The Very Young Wife hurried across the grass. Her face was pink with alarm. She seized Snooky by the arm, struck the cookie from his hand, and then knocked away the other. One landed in the dust. The second broke against the walk.

“You come home this minute.”

“Want it,” Snooky wailed.

“You mustn’t take things from strangers.”

Blanche stood beside the sweet peas. She did not speak.

The Very Young Wife pulled the child through the pickets. Snooky twisted backward, crying after the broken cookie. Before the kitchen door slammed, Blanche had bent to pick up the pieces.

We had watched all this.

Mrs. Dillion said later that the Very Young Wife had done exactly right. Mrs. Pritchard said one could not be too careful. Mrs. Mooney wondered what Blanche expected, offering sweets to children.

I remember the blue saucer in Blanche’s hand. I remember how she brushed the dust from the walnut and dropped the pieces, one by one, into her apron pocket.

That summer she preserved everything that would consent to enter a jar. Strawberries in June, cherries in July, peaches and tomatoes in August. Her kitchen steamed from morning until evening. Rows of glass jars accumulated in the pantry, glowing ruby, amber, and gold. We could see them when the back door stood open.

“She can’t eat all that,” said Mrs. Dillion.

“She’s used to feeding a crowd,” said Mrs. Pritchard.

That remark traveled through the neighborhood and reached Blanche. We knew it had reached her because the next morning her back door was shut.

By autumn she had ceased saying good morning.

Not rudely. Blanche was never rude. She simply lowered her head and passed. She ordered groceries by telephone. She changed pews—then stopped going to church. She still kept the house immaculate, still worked in the garden, still set a lamp in the front window at dusk. But something had withdrawn behind her face. The cottage remained open; Blanche herself had begun to close.

Winter came early.

The first snow fell before Thanksgiving, wet and heavy, bending the bare branches. By January, Sycamore Street lay between banks of frozen gray snow, and smoke descended from the chimneys instead of rising. The men complained of coal prices. Children coasted on Emery Hill. Women compared colds.

One Saturday the Very Young Husband went to Centerville to buy machinery for the feed business. He intended to return by evening. At four o’clock the wind shifted north. Snow began as a dry whisper and thickened until houses across the street disappeared. By six the streetcars had stopped. By eight every road out of town was blocked.

The storm did not fall; it attacked. It clawed under doors, screamed at eaves, hurled handfuls of ice against windows. Trees cracked. Telephone wires sagged and snapped. The electric lights failed, returned weakly, and failed again.

We stayed inside beside our furnaces. We lighted lamps, brought blankets downstairs, and said we had not seen such a night since the blizzard of ’09.

At the gray cottage, Snooky was sick.

He had awakened from his nap with a cold, and by supper his cheeks burned. The Very Young Wife gave him syrup and rocked him. At nine he began to cough—a harsh, barking cough that seemed too large and terrible to come from his small body.

She telephoned Doctor Hall.

The line was dead.

She tried Mrs. Dillion. No answer. The wind had torn down the neighborhood wires. She wrapped Snooky in a blanket and carried him from room to room, crying almost as hard as he did. His breath came with a sawing sound. He fought the blanket. His lips darkened.

The Very Young Wife knew only that her baby could not breathe and that her husband was twenty miles away behind walls of snow.

She ran onto the porch and screamed for help.

The storm swallowed her voice.

Mrs. Dillion’s house was nearest on the other side, but the snow between the two porches had drifted waist-high. No light showed downstairs. The Dillions had gone to bed early after banking the furnace.

Then the Very Young Wife saw a yellow square next door.

Blanche’s kitchen window.

She hesitated.

Even then, with Snooky gasping in her arms, she hesitated. Habit is stronger than reason and sometimes stronger than love. For months she had guarded her steps, her speech, her child’s hands, from crossing that property line.

Snooky coughed again.

She plunged into the snow.

Blanche opened the door before the young mother knocked. She wore a red flannel wrapper and had a lamp in one hand.

“What is it?”

“It’s Snooky. He’s—he can’t—Oh, please, please come!”

Blanche set down the lamp. The Very Young Wife saw her face change—not with surprise, but with an old recognition.

“Bring him in.”

“No—the house—he’s in his bed.”

“Then get back to him. I’m coming.”

Blanche pulled on boots, flung a shawl over her wrapper, and followed through the storm. Inside the gray cottage Snooky lay twisting in his mother’s arms. The sound of his breathing filled the room.

Blanche touched his forehead, opened his mouth, listened at his chest.

“Croup,” she said. “Put him down.”

“Is he going to die?”

“Not if we can help it. Stop crying. He needs you useful.”

The Very Young Wife stared at her.

“Get every kettle you have on the stove. Fill the wash boiler. Shut that window and open the door to the kitchen. Have you kerosene?”

“Yes.”

“Light all the burners. We need steam. Move!”

There was authority in Blanche’s voice, and the girl obeyed.

Blanche carried Snooky into the kitchen. She wrapped him lightly and held him upright against her shoulder. Between coughs she spoke to him in a low, steady murmur.

“That’s it, boy. Easy now. Don’t fight every breath. Save your strength. Lady’s got you.”

The kitchen became hot and wet. Kettles rattled. Steam clouded the windows and curled along the ceiling. Blanche made a tent of sheets over the table, placed steaming pans beneath it, and sat inside with the child while his mother heated more water.

“Doctor,” the Very Young Wife kept saying. “We’ve got to get a doctor.”

“No one can get through that storm.”

“We could try Mr. Dillion.”

“Try him, then. But put your coat on.”

The girl stumbled into the snow. She reached the Dillion house, beat at the door, and roused the whole family. Mr. Dillion attempted the telephone. Mrs. Dillion sent her eldest boy toward Doctor Hall’s on skis, though he returned after two blocks, blinded and half frozen. We woke then, house by house, and lamps bloomed along Sycamore Street.

We learned that Snooky was ill.

We learned that Blanche Devine was with him.

And, astonishingly, this second fact appeared almost as urgent as the first.

“Her?” said Mrs. Pritchard over the party line, which had revived fitfully.

“What does she know about sick children?”

Mrs. Mooney asked whether somebody respectable ought to go over.

But the storm was severe, and respectable people must consider pneumonia.

Blanche stayed.

For an hour Snooky grew worse. His little chest labored. He clawed at the neck of his nightshirt. The Very Young Wife began to sway.

“Don’t you faint,” Blanche snapped. “If you faint, I’ll put you in the snowbank and leave you there.”

The girl steadied herself against the stove.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry. Bring that basin.”

Blanche tried steam, hot cloths, syrup of ipecac from the medicine cupboard, and a poultice made with onions and something pungent from her own house. She sent Mr. Dillion, who had finally fought his way across, back for mustard, more oil, and a bottle of whiskey.

“Whiskey!” Mrs. Dillion exclaimed.

“For rubbing,” Blanche said. “Though if that husband of yours keeps standing in the doorway, I may drink it.”

Mr. Dillion moved.

Near midnight Snooky seemed to stop breathing.

His mother screamed.

Blanche laid the child across her knees, worked with quick fingers at his throat, turned him, struck gently but firmly between his shoulders, and bent her face close to his. For several dreadful seconds there was only the wind and the girl’s sobbing.

Then Snooky drew a thin, tearing breath.

Blanche’s shoulders sagged. She pressed her mouth against the child’s damp hair.

“The baby,” she whispered. “Oh, the baby.”

The Very Young Wife heard.

“So you—you’ve done this before?”

Blanche did not answer at once. She wiped Snooky’s mouth and shifted him upright.

“My little girl had it.”

“Did she get well?”

“No.”

The word lay quietly in the steaming kitchen.

“I was seventeen,” Blanche went on. “There wasn’t any doctor where we were. Nobody came. She died before morning.”

She said no more. She did not need to. We had demanded explanations of Blanche for years—names, dates, sins, causes—and received them with relish from anyone except Blanche. Yet here, in the wet lamplight, she gave the Very Young Wife the only history that mattered.

“My baby died.”

The girl reached toward her, then drew back. Perhaps the movement was habit. Perhaps fear. Perhaps only exhaustion.

Blanche saw it.

She adjusted the blanket around Snooky and said, “Heat more water.”

Toward two o’clock the storm began to weaken. The wind still beat at the house, but less furiously. Snooky’s breathing eased by degrees so slight that only Blanche trusted them. The terrible bark softened. His clenched hands opened.

At three he slept.

Blanche did not. She sat in the rocking chair with Snooky against her breast and watched each breath. The Very Young Wife knelt beside them, her head on Blanche’s knee.

At dawn Doctor Hall arrived behind a team of plow horses. He stamped snow from his boots, listened to Snooky’s chest, examined the steaming kitchen, and looked at Blanche.

“You’ve done the right things.”

“Is he safe?”

“He will be.”

The Very Young Wife began to cry again, but quietly now. Blanche transferred Snooky into her arms. For a moment the child stirred and clung to Blanche’s wrapper.

“Lady,” he murmured.

Blanche loosened his fingers one by one.

She went home through the blue morning. Her red wrapper showed below the coat she had thrown over it. Her hair hung down her back. She had no hat, and the snow had stopped.

We saw her cross the yard.

Several of us were at our windows.

No one opened a door.

The Very Young Husband returned that afternoon on a freight engine sent through after the plow. He rushed into the gray cottage, heard the story, kissed Snooky, embraced his wife, thanked Doctor Hall, and then asked several questions about Blanche.

“She stayed all night?”

“She saved him,” said the Very Young Wife.

“The doctor saved him.”

“The doctor said she’d done everything.”

The Very Young Husband walked to the window. Blanche’s cottage stood bright against the snow. Smoke rose from its chimney.

“I don’t like it.”

His wife stared.

“You don’t like what?”

“I don’t like your being mixed up with her.”

“Mixed up! Snooky was dying.”

“You could’ve gone to the Dillions.”

“I tried. Blanche was here first.”

“Well, it’s done. But that’s the end of it.”

The Very Young Wife’s face changed. She had spent the night obeying Blanche, watching Blanche fight for her child, hearing about a dead baby no one had helped. For perhaps half a minute she possessed a courage larger than her upbringing.

“I’m going over to thank her.”

“You already thanked her.”

“I didn’t. Not properly.”

“I won’t have it.”

“She saved our boy!”

He lowered his voice, which men often do when saying something brutal they wish to call reasonable.

“Listen. You’re young. You don’t understand these things. A woman like that takes advantage of any opening. You speak to her once, next she’ll be coming over. People will talk. I’ve got a position in this town.”

The Very Young Wife looked down at Snooky.

Her courage lasted another few seconds.

Then it went out.

Three days later the young couple took Snooky for an airing. He was bundled in blankets and seated in his little sled. The sun shone on the snow with a hard brilliance. Blanche sat on her porch, though the air was cold. She wore a plain brown dress and knitted something blue.

The family approached along the walk.

Blanche stood.

The Very Young Husband looked straight ahead. The Very Young Wife bent to adjust Snooky’s blanket, though it needed no adjusting.

Snooky saw Blanche.

“Lady!” he cried.

His father pulled the sled faster.

Blanche remained standing until they passed. Then she sat down. The blue knitting slid from her lap into the snow, and for a while she did not pick it up.

I wish one of us had called to her then.

It would have required so little. A wave. A nod. Two ordinary words sent across the white fence: Good morning.

We did not.

In March a wagon came for Blanche’s furniture.

The maple rocker went first, then the white sewing table, the cream curtains, the yellow dishes, the great carved bed. The men carried out boxes of preserves. One dropped a jar, and peaches burst upon the walk in a glitter of syrup and broken glass.

Blanche sold the cottage for less than she had paid.

On her last morning she walked through the garden. Snow still lay in the shaded corners, but green points of tulips had pushed through beside the porch. She paused at the fence where Snooky had entered for cookies. Then she went inside and shut the door.

When she came out again she wore the dark fur coat and the diamond earrings. Her shoes had high, narrow heels. The scent of violets drifted after her.

A hired automobile carried her toward the freight tracks.

Within a month the red curtains were up again at the old house. Men who would not bow to Blanche on Sycamore Street found the road beyond the tracks passable after dark. The Very Young Husband was seen there once, though he explained that his automobile had developed engine trouble.

The cottage was sold to a bank clerk and his wife. Mrs. Dillion took them a pie. Mrs. Pritchard invited the wife to the church circle. The Very Young Wife called with Snooky.

We welcomed them thoroughly.

As for Blanche, we said what respectable towns have always said when they have pushed someone down and then discovered her fallen.

“I knew she wouldn’t stick it out,” said Mrs. Pritchard.

“You can’t change that sort,” said Mrs. Mooney.

“They always go back,” said the Very Young Husband.

Yes, we said.

They always do.

# The Keeper of Lost Hours

Every town loses time.

A minute slips beneath a café table while someone waits for an apology. An afternoon vanishes in a hospital corridor. Whole summers are misplaced by children who swear they only closed their eyes for a moment.

In Bellwether, lost time gathered beneath the clock tower.

No one knew this except Elias Vale, the tower’s keeper, and he had learned it from his mother, who had learned it from hers. For one hundred and forty-three years, a member of the Vale family had climbed the narrow staircase each night, entered the clock room, and collected whatever the town had let fall.

Usually, there was not much.

A few seconds glittered on the floor like flakes of mica. Minutes clung to the gears in pale threads. Elias drew them carefully into glass bottles, labeled each one by date, and stored them in cabinets built into the tower’s circular walls.

There were thousands of bottles.

Some held only a sigh.

Others contained enough time to boil an egg, mend a stocking, or say something that should have been said before a door closed.

Elias never opened them.

“That is the first rule,” his mother had told him. “Lost time belongs to no one.”

“The second rule?” he had asked.

“Never let the clock stop.”

“And the third?”

She had looked toward the highest cabinet, where the oldest bottles rested under blankets of dust.

“Never return what was willingly given away.”

At twelve years old, Elias had not understood. At fifty-seven, he believed he did.

The people of Bellwether knew him as a tall, quiet man with silver beginning at his temples and a habit of checking his pocket watch during conversation. They waved to him in the market. They called him when mantel clocks ran slow or grandfather clocks began striking thirteen. Children dared one another to knock on the tower door after midnight, though none had ever found the courage.

Elias lived alone in two small rooms beneath the clock. He slept lightly, ate plainly, and kept his memories in better order than most people kept their cupboards.

Then, one autumn evening, a woman named Mara Quinn knocked on his door.

Elias knew who she was. Everyone did.

She had grown up in Bellwether, left at seventeen, and returned three weeks earlier to care for her father, who was dying. In her youth, she had been famous for climbing rooftops and swimming in the river during storms. Now she was forty, perhaps, with rain-dark hair and a red coat that seemed too bright for the gray evening.

“I need an hour,” she said when Elias opened the door.

Most people began with good evening.

“I repair clocks,” he replied.

“You keep lost time.”

The rain ticked against the streetlamps. Somewhere above them, the tower mechanism shifted with a heavy iron sigh.

Elias held the door halfway closed. “Who told you that?”

“My father.”

“Daniel Quinn tells stories.”

“He is dying.”

“Dying people tell stories too.”

Mara stepped closer. Her face was pale from lack of sleep, but her eyes were steady.

“He said your mother gave him seven minutes in 1982. He had missed the last bus from Stonebridge, and those seven minutes let him reach it before it left. If he hadn’t caught that bus, he wouldn’t have met my mother.”

Elias said nothing.

The story was true.

His mother had broken the first rule only once, as far as he knew. Daniel Quinn had arrived at the tower on a winter night, frantic and shivering. Elias had been a boy then, listening from the stairs. His mother had opened a bottle and poured seven minutes into the clock.

For those inside the tower, nothing happened. Outside, the town drew backward like a breath. Snow rose from footprints. Chimney smoke folded into brick. The bus returned to the station, and Daniel ran.

Elias remembered his mother weeping afterward.

“Seven minutes,” Mara continued. “That is all he told me. He made me promise not to ask until I truly needed it.”

“And now you need an hour.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“My father cannot speak anymore. He tried this morning, but the words wouldn’t come. The doctor says he may not wake tomorrow.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I don’t want your sorrow.”

“Most people don’t. They ask for it anyway.”

Her jaw tightened. “I argued with him the last time he could talk. I told him he had driven everyone away. I told him my mother died miserable because of him.”

“Was it true?”

“Some of it.”

“And you want to unsay it.”

“I want one hour before I said it. One hour while he was still himself.”

Elias looked up the spiral staircase behind him. The clock struck six, each bell rolling through the walls and into his bones.

“One hour is not a small thing,” he said.

“It is to you.”

“No. It never is.”

She reached into her coat and produced a silver wristwatch. Its face was cracked, its hands frozen at 4:17.

“My mother’s,” she said. “Payment.”

“I don’t sell time.”

“Then take mine.”

Elias looked at her.

“Take an hour from me,” Mara said. “A year. Whatever is fair.”

“There is no fair exchange.”

“Then make an unfair one.”

He should have closed the door. Instead, he noticed the wristwatch’s second hand trembling beneath the cracked glass, trying and failing to advance.

“Come back tomorrow,” he said.

“He may not have tomorrow.”

“Neither may you.”

“That has always been true.”

She met his eyes until he looked away.

“Midnight,” Elias said. “Come alone.”

After she left, he climbed to the clock room.

The great mechanism filled most of the chamber, a forest of brass wheels and black iron rods. Pendulums swung through wells in the floor. Moonlight shone through four enormous clock faces, painting the room in milky circles.

The bottles whispered in their cabinets.

Lost time was never silent. When enough of it gathered, it murmured with fragments of what had been abandoned.

A spoon striking a saucer.

A baby’s first laugh, unheard by a sleeping father.

Rain on a wedding morning.

The final note of a song interrupted by war.

Elias passed shelves labeled by year until he found the current month. Three weeks earlier, on the day Daniel Quinn had suffered his first seizure, the town had lost nearly four hours. Most of it had pooled in the hospital: time surrendered in waiting rooms, time buried in helplessness, time people wished would pass quickly and then begged to have back.

Among the bottles was one containing sixty-three minutes.

The glass was warm.

Elias carried it to his worktable. He told himself he was only examining it, but he had told himself many small lies during his life, and he recognized the shape of another.

At eleven minutes past midnight, Mara arrived.

“You’re late,” he said.

“My father woke. I stayed until he slept again.”

“Then perhaps you have already found what you wanted.”

“No.”

Elias led her upstairs.

She paused when she saw the clock room. The machinery moved around her with stately indifference. Behind the glass faces, the town lay under a black sky, roofs shining after rain.

“So much,” she whispered, looking at the cabinets.

“Most is unusable.”

“Why?”

“A lost second can be restored easily. An hour resists. A day might tear the clock apart.”

“You said might.”

He ignored that.

On the table, the bottle glowed faintly. Mara reached for it, but Elias caught her wrist.

“You must understand what happens.”

“I go back.”

“No. The town goes back. Everyone within sound of the tower bells returns to where they were one hour ago. Their bodies, their words, the rain in the gutters—everything. But only you and I will remember.”

“Why you?”

“The clock remembers its keeper.”

“And why me?”

“Because you will drink the hour.”

For the first time, her resolve flickered. “Drink it?”

“It will taste like nothing you know. Afterward, the clock will strike backward. When it stops, you will have one hour before the old moment arrives again.”

“Then I can change it.”

“You can try.”

“Try?”

“Time is not a road, Mara. It does not enjoy being walked twice.”

She pulled her wrist free. “You helped my father.”

“My mother did.”

“So help me.”

Elias turned the bottle in his hands. Pale light moved inside it like mist.

“There is a price,” he said. “Not one I choose. When the hour is restored, another hour will be taken from you.”

“You told me there was no fair exchange.”

“There isn’t. The clock may take an hour from the end of your life, or from a morning years from now. It may take an hour you treasure.”

“Will I know?”

“No.”

“Then open it.”

He removed the stopper.

The whispers in the room ceased. Even the pendulum seemed to hesitate.

Mara raised the bottle and drank.

The light vanished down her throat.

Above them, the first bell struck.

Its note was wrong—deep and inverted, more felt than heard. The clock hands shuddered and began to turn backward.

A second bell sounded.

Beyond the glass faces, chimney smoke sank. Fallen leaves lifted from pavements and fastened themselves to branches. A cat leaped backward onto a wall. Rain flew upward from the river in silver needles.

Mara gripped the table.

Bell after bell, the town unwound.

Elias watched the minute hand retreat. He had seen time restored only once, and that childhood memory had softened at the edges. He had forgotten the terror of it: the sense that the world was a tapestry being pulled thread by thread through the eye of a needle.

At last, the clock stopped.

The hands showed 4:02 in the afternoon.

Sunlight replaced midnight.

Mara stood beside him, still wearing her red coat, though she had not been wearing it at 4:02. The returned hour clung around her like a transparent flame.

“You have until 5:02,” Elias said.

She ran.

Elias remained in the clock room, listening.

The bells did not move. The gears were locked, though the pendulum swung. Across Bellwether, people repeated their hour without knowing it. Bakers returned bread to ovens. Teachers erased the same chalkboards. Lovers spoke familiar lies with fresh conviction.

Elias went to the eastern clock face and looked down.

Mara crossed the square, dodging people who seemed to her unbearably slow. She reached the hospital and disappeared through its doors.

On the table, the empty bottle cracked.

A thin line appeared from neck to base.

Elias stared at it.

His mother had told him that cracked glass meant the returned time had been rejected. The hour would not settle cleanly. Something within it had changed too greatly—or had never wanted to be changed at all.

He went to the mechanism. A small gear near the escapement was turning forward while every other wheel remained still.

“That is impossible,” he murmured.

The gear spun faster.

From the cabinets came a sudden rattling. Hundreds of bottles shook on their shelves. Lost seconds flared in the glass like trapped stars.

Then a voice spoke behind him.

“Elias.”

He turned.

His mother stood beside the stairs.

She looked as she had on the night she died: seventy-two, thin as winter, wearing her blue house dress. One hand rested over her heart. Her gray braid fell across her shoulder.

Elias could not breathe.

“You let the clock stop,” she said.

“You’re not here.”

“No.”

“You’re a memory.”

“Yes.”

“Whose?”

She glanced at the cabinets. “Everyone’s.”

The bottles rattled harder. Elias backed toward the worktable.

“What is happening?”

“The hour is looking for somewhere to go.”

“It belongs to Mara.”

“Not all of it.”

His mother’s image flickered, and for an instant Elias saw dozens of faces layered over hers: strangers, neighbors, children grown old, old people made young.

“Time given away willingly cannot be returned,” she said.

“The third rule.”

“You remembered the words.”

“Not the meaning.”

“No.”

The spinning gear screamed.

“What did Mara’s father give away?” Elias asked.

His mother looked toward the town. “An hour.”

“When?”

“Forty years ago.”

Elias understood.

Seven minutes had allowed Daniel Quinn to catch the bus, but a restored moment demanded its price. The clock had taken an hour from him sometime later. An hour he had surrendered, perhaps gladly, perhaps without knowing.

And now Mara had swallowed an hour gathered on the day of his illness.

“Is it the same hour?” Elias asked.

“Partly.”

“What happens if she returns it?”

“The clock will take back the gift.”

“What gift?”

But the apparition had already begun to fade.

“Mother.”

Her expression softened.

“You should have left Bellwether,” she said.

“You needed me.”

“No. The clock did.”

Then she vanished.

Elias stood alone.

At 4:39, he left the tower and ran to the hospital.

The repeated afternoon had an unreal brightness. People moved through it like actors in a play he had seen too many times. Mrs. Farrow dropped a bag of apples outside the grocer’s. Elias knew she had dropped them before, because he had seen one bruised apple in the gutter that evening. A cyclist shouted at a delivery van. A dog barked from an upstairs window.

At the hospital, Elias found Mara in Room 12, seated beside her father.

Daniel Quinn looked smaller than Elias remembered. Illness had hollowed his cheeks, but his eyes were open and clear.

Mara held his hand.

“You came,” she said.

Daniel turned his head slowly. “Clock keeper.”

His voice was weak, but it was a voice.

Elias glanced at the wall clock.

4:44.

“You told him?” Mara asked.

“Not yet,” Daniel whispered.

“Told me what?”

Daniel closed his eyes, gathering strength. “Your mother.”

Mara stiffened.

“She wasn’t on the bus,” he said.

“You met her on the bus.”

“No.”

“You always said—”

“I saw her at the station. She was waiting for the same bus. But when time turned back, the bus returned. I ran for it.” He swallowed painfully. “She didn’t.”

Mara looked at Elias.

“My mother returned seven minutes,” he said.

Daniel nodded. “I saw the clock run backward. Thought I’d gone mad. Then the bus was there, and I got on. Through the window, I saw Anna walking away.”

“But you met her.”

“Next morning. I found her at the boardinghouse. Asked her to breakfast.” A tired smile moved across his face. “She said any man foolish enough to chase a stranger deserved coffee.”

Mara’s grip loosened around his hand. “You lied all these years.”

“I made the story simpler.”

“You make everything simpler by making it false.”

“Mara,” Elias warned.

She looked at the clock.

4:51.

“I came back to apologize,” she said. “Not to do this again.”

Daniel watched her with the calm of someone standing beyond defense. “Then don’t.”

Silence filled the room.

Outside, a trolley rolled past. Somewhere down the corridor, a metal tray struck the floor. Elias remembered hearing the same crash earlier that day.

Mara leaned closer to her father.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “What I told you before—I wanted to hurt you.”

“You did.”

“I know.”

“You were not wrong.”

“That doesn’t make it better.”

“No.”

She waited, perhaps expecting forgiveness to arrive like a doctor called from another room.

Daniel drew a breath. “Your mother was unhappy near the end.”

Mara’s eyes filled.

“So was I,” he continued. “We loved each other badly for a long time. Then we stopped knowing how to stop.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I thought if you blamed me, you could keep loving her.”

“I could have loved both of you.”

“I know that now.”

The clock showed 4:57.

Elias stepped forward. “Mara, the hour is unstable.”

“What does that mean?”

“It may take more than it promised.”

“How much more?”

“I don’t know.”

Daniel looked from one to the other. “You turned it back for her?”

“Yes,” Elias said.

A shadow of anger crossed the old man’s face. “Fool.”

“I have heard that before.”

Daniel gripped Mara’s hand with sudden strength. “Leave.”

“No.”

“You said what you came to say.”

“I still have five minutes.”

“Those five minutes are not yours.”

Mara began to cry then, silently and helplessly.

Daniel lifted her hand to his lips.

“Go,” he whispered. “Let something end.”

At 4:59, Elias and Mara left the room.

They stood in the corridor while the wall clock advanced. Mara leaned against the wall, trembling.

“What happens at 5:02?” she asked.

“The two hours meet.”

“And my father?”

“I don’t know.”

She laughed bitterly. “You say that often for a man who keeps time.”

“A keeper is not a master.”

The second hand moved.

5:01.

From the tower, far across town, came a low metallic groan.

Lights flickered overhead. The corridor lengthened, then snapped back. Nurses repeated half-steps. A doctor emerged from an elevator twice.

Mara seized Elias’s sleeve. “Can we stop it?”

“No.”

“Can we give the hour back?”

“He gave part of it away willingly. It cannot be returned.”

“Then where does it go?”

Elias thought of the cracked bottle, the spinning gear, his mother’s face.

“Somewhere empty,” he said.

The clock reached 5:02.

The tower bell struck.

The hospital vanished.

For one impossible instant, Elias stood in a darkness filled with doors.

Thousands of them stretched in every direction: red doors, wooden doors, doors painted blue, doors without handles. Behind each waited an hour someone had lost. He heard laughter, arguments, lullabies, final breaths. He saw his own life divided into bright rooms.

In one, he was twenty-three and boarding a train from Bellwether.

In another, he was forty, holding the hand of a woman he had never met.

In another, he sat beside his mother as she died, not beneath the tower winding the clock.

All the hours he might have lived.

All willingly surrendered.

The returned hour rushed out of Mara in a ribbon of white fire. It searched among the doors, rejected one, then another.

At last it found an open room.

Elias knew it at once.

It was the hour after his mother’s funeral, when he had climbed the tower, looked out across Bellwether, and decided to remain its keeper forever. He had given that hour—and every hour after it—to the clock willingly.

The white fire entered.

The door closed.

Then the hospital returned.

Mara was on her knees. Elias lay beside her.

The wall clock read 5:03.

For several seconds, neither moved.

A nurse ran past them into Room 12. Mara followed. Elias remained in the corridor, too weak to stand.

He heard no alarm from the room, no shouted demand for equipment. Only quiet voices, and then Mara’s grief—soft, broken, real.

Daniel Quinn had died at 5:02, as he had the first time.

The hour had changed nothing.

And yet, Elias thought, that was not true.

Somewhere beneath the pain, a knot had been untied.

He looked at his hands. They seemed younger. The veins had faded. The ache in his knuckles was gone.

A silver wristwatch lay on the floor beside him.

Its cracked face showed 4:17.

Then the second hand moved.

Elias picked it up.

When he returned to the tower, dawn was beginning to thin the sky.

The clock had restarted. Bottles stood peacefully in their cabinets. The empty glass on the worktable had broken into two clean pieces.

Elias climbed to the highest platform and opened a narrow door he had never opened before.

Cold morning air entered the tower.

Below, Bellwether stirred. A bakery lit its ovens. Street sweepers gathered wet leaves. In the hospital, Mara sat beside her father for the final time. The town continued, spending what it had and losing what it could not hold.

Elias placed Mara’s wristwatch on the table.

Then he took off his keeper’s coat.

By sunrise, he had packed one bag.

He did not know how many years the clock had returned to him, nor how many waited beyond the town. He did not know who would climb the stairs that night or whether anyone should.

For the first time in his life, uncertainty did not frighten him.

At the station, Mara stood beneath the iron awning in her red coat.

“I thought you might come,” she said.

“Why?”

“You left my mother’s watch at the hospital.”

“I repaired it.”

She held it up. The second hand moved steadily.

“Where are you going?” she asked.

Elias looked at the timetable. There were trains to Stonebridge, to the coast, to cities whose towers kept ordinary clocks.

“I don’t know.”

Mara nodded as if this were an excellent destination.

The train arrived at 7:10.

Neither of them hurried, but they reached it before the doors closed.
